sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Maitreya** ​(*maitreya*) — ‌Future Buddha, ‌Loving-Kindness · ​'The Benevolent ​One' ​— the ​Bodhisattva who ​will return ‌as ​the future ​Buddha — ‌belongs to ​the Buddhist ‌tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under the ​domain "Future ​Buddha, ​Loving-Kindness". The ​name means ‌"'The Benevolent ​One' ‌— the ​Bodhisattva who ‌will return ​as the ‌future ​Buddha"[^1].

**Maitreya** ‌is the ​**Buddha of ​the ‌future** — ‌now a ‌bodhisattva enthroned ​in Tuṣita ​heaven, ‌waiting for ​the Dharma's ​decline to ‌run its ​course. ​His name ‌is his ​program: maitrī, ‌**loving-kindness**, ​the first ​of the ​four immeasurables ​— a ‌promise ‌that the ​wheel, having ‌turned down, ​will turn ​up ‌again.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌records the ‌canonical scholarly ‌spelling ​**Maitreya** and ‌serves its ​temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/maitreya/). ​The ‌displayed form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description ‌computed from ​the displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII ​form *maitreya* ‌contains the ​same letters: ‌no recovered ​diacritics ‌or special ‌encoding is ​claimed. The ​work ​here is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Devanagari ​as ​**मैत्रेय**. Etymologically ​it ​means ​"'The Benevolent ‌One' ​— the ​Bodhisattva ‌who will ​return ‌as the ​future ‌Buddha"[^1].

The ​canonical ​spelling **Maitreya** ​matches ​the conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization. ​The plain ‌ASCII ​form *maitreya* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters, ​so no ‌lost ​diacritics or ​encoding ‌transition is ‌claimed. ‌The editorial ​work ​is ‌to fix ​one ​reviewed reference ‌spelling, ​preserve capitalization ​and ‌provenance, and ​keep ‌the original ​evidence ​visible. The ​displayed ​form is ‌ASCII-equivalent ‌— ​a description ‌computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form itself.

‌The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ​**m** → ‌**M** ​— Same, ​capitalized
- ​**a** → ‌**a** ​— ​Same
- **i** ​→ ‌**i** — ​Same
- ​**t** → ​**t** ‌— Same
- ​**r** ‌→ **r** ​— ‌Same
- **e** ​→ ‌**e** — ‌Same
- ​**y** ​→ **y** ​— ​Same
- **a** ‌→ ‌**a** — ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/maitreya/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**maitreya** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Maitreya.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Maitreya" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Maitreya" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"maitreya" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Maitreya ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Maitreya ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Maitreya ‌place future ​buddha, ​loving-kindness at ​the ​center of ​a ‌living mythological ​world.

### ​Origins (Myth)

‌Maitreya ​appears in ‌buddhist ​tradition as ‌future ​buddha, loving-kindness. ​The ​name's meaning, ​"'The ​Benevolent One' ‌— ​the ‌Bodhisattva who ​will ‌return as ​the ‌future Buddha", ​shapes ‌the narratives ​told ​about this ‌figure.

### ‌Worship and ‌Memory ​(Cult)

Devotees ​and ‌later tradition-keepers ​preserved ​Maitreya in ‌ritual, ​text, and ​iconography, ‌ensuring the ​name ‌survived into ​the ​modern scholarly ​record.

​The myths ‌of ‌Maitreya survive ​in ‌fragments, summaries, ​and ​later retellings. ‌Each ‌version reflects ‌the ‌interests of ​its ‌tellers — ​poets, ​priests, philosophers, ​and ‌scholars. ​The PuniCodex ​entry ​does not ‌privilege ​a single ​version; ​it gathers ‌the ​attestations so ‌that ​readers can ‌compare ​them. The ‌restoration ‌Maitreya gives ​the ​figure a ​stable ​name around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet assigned ​to ‌Maitreya ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Buddhist ​name ‌of this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources section.

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming मैत्रेय, ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains ​tied ​to future ​buddha ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes (name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Every ​religion promises ‌an end; ‌Buddhism alone ​promises ​a **sequel**. ​Maitreya is ​the argument ​that ‌decline is ​not the ​last ‌chapter — ​that the ‌Dharma, having ​dimmed, ‌will be ​re-taught in ​full, by ​a ​teacher already ​named, already ‌enthroned in ​the ‌heaven of ​delight. The ‌figure dissolves ​despair ‌without denying ​decay: the ‌wheel does ​turn ​down, and ‌it turns ‌up ‌again.

He ​is also ​the most ‌human ​of the ​great bodhisattvas ‌because his ​career ​is still ‌open. The ​Buddha's story ‌is ​closed and ​perfect; Maitreya's ​is a ​promise ‌with a ‌waiting room, ​and the ‌tradition ​placed Śākyamuni ​himself in ‌that ‌room before ‌his final ‌birth. To ​venerate ‌Maitreya is ​to admit ​that one's ​own ‌age is ​incomplete — ​and to ​refuse ‌to treat ​incompleteness as ​defeat. The ​future ‌Buddha is ​Buddhism's answer ‌to the ​oldest ‌anxiety: **what ​if it ‌all ‌ends with ​us?** Not, ​says the ​prophecy. ​It ends, ‌and it ‌begins again, ​kinder.[^1]
